Large [[Clade|clade]] of animals characterized by bilateral symmetry during embryonic development. Their body plans are arranged around a longitudinal axis with a front (head) and rear (tail) end, and a left and right side. Nearly all bilaterians are bilaterally symmetrical as adults; the exception is [[Echinoderm|echinoderms]], which have pentaradial symmetry as adults. Most have complete digestive tracts with a separate [[Mouth|mouth]] and [[Anus|anus]], and sense organs and nerve ganglia concentrated at the front end of the body, a feature called cephalization.

Bilaterians form one of five main animal lineages, the others being [[Sponge|sponges]], [[Cnidaria]], Ctenophora and Placozoa. They diversified rapidly in the late [[Ediacaran]] and the [[Cambrian]] and include over 98% of known animal species. Traditionally they are divided into deuterostomes and protostomes, depending on whether the blastopore becomes the anus or the mouth. The phylum Xenacoelomorpha, erected in 2011, does not clearly fit either group.

City (pop., 2024: 347,342) in northern [[Spain]], the largest city in Biscay province and the [[Basque Country (autonomous community)|Basque Country]]. Founded in the late 13th century, it became a commercial hub exporting wool and iron from nearby quarries. Heavy industrialization in the 19th and early 20th centuries made it the center of Spain's second most industrialized region, behind [[Barcelona]]. Its regeneration was started by the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao, designed by [[Frank Gehry]] and opened in 1997, and the city received the 2010 Lee Kuan Yew World City Prize for its urban transformation.

Chinese online video-sharing platform based in [[Shanghai]]. Users upload, view and comment on videos, including through *danmu*, scrolling on-screen comments. The site grew out of a [[Hatsune Miku]] fan community founded in 2009 and was launched as Bilibili in 2010. It began with [[Anime|anime]], comics and games, and later expanded into documentaries, variety shows and original programming, as well as live streaming, mostly of mobile games.

American football coach, head coach of the North Carolina Tar Heels since 2024. He was head coach of the [[New England Patriots]] for 24 seasons from 2000, winning six [[Super Bowl|Super Bowls]], a record for a head coach, along with 17 AFC East titles. Including two Super Bowls as defensive coordinator of the New York Giants, he has won eight, the most of any individual in NFL history. He holds the record for most playoff coaching wins, with 31.

American [[Stand-up comedy|stand-up]] comedian, podcaster, actor and writer. Known for confrontational, observational comedy about social issues and politics, he created, co-wrote and voiced the lead character in the [[Netflix]] animated sitcom *F Is for Family* (2015–2021). He has also had roles in *Breaking Bad* and *The Mandalorian*, and he directed the feature film *Old Dads* (2023). He has received two Emmy Award nominations and two Grammy Award nominations.

American politician and lawyer, 42nd [[President of the United States|president of the United States]] (1993–2001). A [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]] and former governor of Arkansas, he signed the North American Free Trade Agreement, and his presidency saw the longest peacetime economic expansion in U.S. history up to that time. The House of Representatives impeached him in 1998 on charges of perjury and obstruction of justice; the Senate acquitted him in 1999. After leaving office he founded the Clinton Foundation, which addresses causes including [[HIV/AIDS]] and global warming.

American former comedian and actor. He played Cliff Huxtable in the sitcom *The Cosby Show* (1984–1992) and became the first Black actor to win three Primetime Emmy Awards for Best Actor in a Drama Series, for *I Spy*. Over 60 women have accused him of offenses including [[Rape|rape]] and sexual assault; he has maintained his innocence. A 2018 conviction for aggravated sexual assault was vacated in 2021 by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court. In civil cases he was found liable for sexual assault in 2022 and in 2026, the latter with $19 million in damages.

American businessman and philanthropist, co-founder of [[Microsoft]]. With his childhood friend [[Paul Allen]], he founded the software company in 1975 after leaving [[Harvard University|Harvard]]. He served as its chief executive for 25 years and became the world's then-youngest billionaire in 1987, after Microsoft's initial public offering. Forbes ranked him the world's wealthiest person in 18 of the 24 years from 1995 to 2017. He co-chaired the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, the world's largest private charitable organization, with his then-wife, Melinda French Gates, from 2000 until 2024. The foundation focused on health, education and poverty alleviation, including efforts against [[Tuberculosis|tuberculosis]], [[Malaria|malaria]] and [[Polio|polio]]. In 2010 he and [[Warren Buffett]] founded the Giving Pledge, under which billionaires commit to giving at least half their wealth to philanthropy.

American comedian, television host and political commentator. He hosts the HBO political talk show *Real Time with Bill Maher*, which began in 2003, and earlier hosted *Politically Incorrect* on ABC and Comedy Central (1993–2002). Often described as a moderate liberal, he is known for his political satire, and his critical views of religion were the basis for the documentary *Religulous* (2008). He supports [[Animal rights|animal rights]], serving on the board of PETA since 1997, and supports the legalization of [[Cannabis (drug)|cannabis]]. He received a Hollywood Walk of Fame star in 2010.

American actor and comedian known for his deadpan delivery. A cast member of [[Saturday Night Live]] from 1977 to 1980, he starred in comedies including *Caddyshack* (1980), *Ghostbusters* (1984) and *Groundhog Day* (1993). He received a Best Actor Academy Award nomination for *Lost in Translation* (2003). He has acted in ten films by director [[Wes Anderson]], beginning with *Rushmore* (1998), and was awarded the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor in 2016.

American science communicator and former mechanical engineer. He began his career at [[Boeing]] in Seattle, where he invented a hydraulic resonance suppressor tube used on 747 airplanes. As host of *Bill Nye the Science Guy* (1993–1998), he won 19 Emmy Awards from 23 nominations, including Outstanding Performer in Children's Programming. He later served as CEO of The Planetary Society and starred in the [[Netflix]] series *Bill Nye Saves the World*, which ran from 2017 to 2018.

American basketball center and coach. He played for the [[Boston Celtics]] from 1956 to 1969 and won 11 [[National Basketball Association|NBA]] championships, including eight in a row from 1959 to 1966. A five-time NBA Most Valuable Player, he led the league in rebounds four times. In 1969 he became the first Black coach to win an NBA championship, as player-coach of the Celtics. In 2011 [[Barack Obama]] awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom for his accomplishments on the court and in the civil rights movement.

American singer-songwriter. She first gained attention in 2015 with the single "Ocean Eyes", written and produced by her brother, Finneas O'Connell. Her debut album, *When We All Fall Asleep, Where Do We Go?* (2019), topped the Billboard 200. She has won two [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]] for Best Original Song, for "No Time to Die" and "What Was I Made For?", and ten [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]]. She is the first person born in the 21st century to win both a Grammy and an Academy Award.

American [[Jazz|jazz]] and swing singer, nicknamed Lady Day by her music partner Lester Young. Born Eleanora Fagan, she had a difficult childhood in Baltimore, began singing in Harlem nightclubs and signed with Brunswick in 1935. Her recording with Teddy Wilson of "What a Little Moonlight Can Do" became a jazz standard. Her performance of "Strange Fruit", a song against [[Lynching|lynching]], became one of her signature recordings. Drug abuse and legal troubles in the late 1940s led to a short prison sentence, after which she performed sold-out concerts at Carnegie Hall. She died of cirrhosis and heart failure. Her four Grammy Awards were all posthumous, and she was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2000 as an early influence.

City (pop., 2020: 117,116) in south-central [[Montana]], the state's largest city and the seat of Yellowstone County. Founded in March 1882 as a railroad town named for Frederick H. Billings, a former president of the Northern Pacific Railroad, it was nicknamed the Magic City for its rapid growth. It is the trade and distribution center for much of eastern Montana. The Billings area's population grew 89% from 1969 to 2021, compared with 59% statewide. The northeast entrance of [[Yellowstone National Park]] lies a little over 100 miles (160 km) away.

American actor, filmmaker and singer-songwriter. He wrote, directed and starred in the independent drama *Sling Blade* (1996), for which he won an Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay and was nominated for Best Actor. He won a Golden Globe for playing Lorne Malvo in the television series *Fargo* (2014) and starred in the Paramount+ series *Landman* from 2024. He has been married six times, including to [[Angelina Jolie]] from 2000 to 2003.

Scottish actor, musician and retired [[Stand-up comedy|stand-up]] comedian, known as the Big Yin. He began as a [[Folk music|folk]] singer with the Humblebums and became a comedian in the early 1970s, known for improvised observational comedy with strong language. His single "D.I.V.O.R.C.E." reached No. 1 on the UK Singles Chart in 1975. He was knighted in 2017 for services to entertainment and charity. He announced his retirement from comedy in 2018 and has since established himself as an artist.

American comedian, actor and filmmaker. He gained prominence as Jodie Dallas on the ABC sitcom *Soap* (1977–1981) and was a cast member of [[Saturday Night Live]] from 1984 to 1985. His films include *When Harry Met Sally...* (1989) and *City Slickers* (1991), and he voices Mike Wazowski in [[Pixar|Pixar]]'s *Monsters, Inc.* franchise. He has hosted the [[Academy Awards]] nine times. His one-man show *700 Sundays* won a Tony Award in 2004, and he has received six Primetime Emmy Awards.

American evangelist and ordained Southern Baptist minister, and a civil rights advocate. From the late 1940s he preached live sermons in stadiums around the world, broadcast by radio and television, and he held annual crusades from 1947 until his retirement in 2005. He hosted the radio show *Hour of Decision* from 1950 to 1954. He insisted on racial integration at his revivals as early as 1953, and in 1957 invited [[Martin Luther King Jr.]] to preach jointly at a New York revival. He was close to presidents Dwight D. Eisenhower, Lyndon B. Johnson and [[Richard Nixon]]. He was named on Gallup's list of most admired men and women a record 61 times. In 2002, remarks about Jewish influence in the media that he had made in 1972 Oval Office conversations with Nixon became public, and he apologized.

American singer, songwriter and pianist, nicknamed the Piano Man after his 1973 signature song. His album *The Stranger* (1977) sold over 10 million copies and was Columbia Records' best-selling release. *52nd Street* (1978) won the [[Grammy Awards|Grammy]] for Album of the Year. Joel has sold more than 160 million records worldwide. He performed a record-breaking residency at [[Madison Square Garden]] from 2014 to 2024.

Austrian and American film director and screenwriter. Born Samuel Wilder in Sucha, Galicia, Austria-Hungary, he worked as a journalist in Vienna and began screenwriting in [[Berlin|Berlin]]. After the rise of the [[Nazi Party|Nazi Party]] he moved to Paris, and in 1934 to Hollywood. He co-wrote the screenplay for *Ninotchka* (1939) and co-wrote the film noir *Double Indemnity* (1944) with [[Raymond Chandler]]. He directed [[Marilyn Monroe]] in *The Seven Year Itch* (1955) and *Some Like It Hot* (1959). He co-wrote, produced and directed *The Apartment* (1960), which won [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]] for Best Picture, Best Director and Best Original Screenplay. He received seven Academy Awards from 21 nominations, and his career spanned five decades.

American outlaw and gunfighter of the Old West. Born Henry McCarty, he used the name William H. Bonney and was linked to nine murders, solely responsible for four. He took part in the Lincoln County War in [[New Mexico]] in 1878. Convicted of a sheriff's murder and sentenced to hang, he escaped jail by killing two deputies, and was then shot dead by Sheriff Pat Garrett at Fort Sumner. Stories that he had survived spread afterward, and more than 50 films have featured him, making him a fixture of the [[Western (genre)|western]] genre.

Number expressed in the base-2 numeral system, which uses only the symbols 0 and 1. Each digit is called a [[Bit|bit]]. Because binary is simple to implement in digital circuits using [[Logic gate|logic gates]], almost all modern [[Computer|computers]] use it. Binary-like systems appeared in ancient cultures: Egyptian Horus-Eye fractions were a binary system for fractional quantities of grain and liquids, and the Chinese [[I Ching]] used hexagrams analogous to three- and six-bit binary numerals. The modern binary system was first studied in Europe by Thomas Harriot in the 15th to 17th centuries, and Gottfried Leibniz is credited with its invention. A binary number may also be a [[Rational number|rational number]] with a finite binary representation, the quotient of an integer by a power of two.

Pair of stars gravitationally bound to, and orbiting, each other. Binary stars are among the most important objects in astrophysics because they allow direct measurement of stellar masses and tests of theories of stellar evolution. Stars that appear single to the naked eye but are resolved by a telescope are called visual binaries. Others are detected by [[Spectroscopy|spectroscopy]] or [[Astrometry|astrometry]], and eclipsing binaries have orbits aligned with the line of sight, so their stars eclipse each other. Close binaries can exchange mass, and binaries are progenitors of [[Nova|novae]] and type Ia [[Supernova|supernovae]]. The term was first used by [[William Herschel]] in 1802. The first orbit of a binary star was computed in 1827 by Félix Savary, for Xi Ursae Majoris. The Washington Double Star Catalog lists over 100,000 double stars, but orbits are known for only a few thousand of them.

Smallest amount of energy needed to remove a particle from a system of particles, or to disassemble the system into its individual parts. The term is mainly used in condensed matter physics, atomic physics and chemistry, while [[Nuclear physics|nuclear physics]] uses separation energy. A bound system typically has lower energy than its unbound constituents, and a decrease in total energy ΔE comes with a decrease in mass Δm, where Δmc² = ΔE. In a nucleus, binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56, at about 8.8 MeV, and falls for heavier elements, so fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei both release energy. For an [[Atom|atom]], binding energy is the energy needed to remove an electron; in hydrogen it is 13.6 eV.
